Alloy 454 is an alloy that exclusively uses single crystals.
The standard compositions of the reference alloys Mar-M 200 and Mar-M 247 are shown in Table 1.
Alloy 454 was solution treated at 1280°C for 4 hours and aged for 32 hours at 871°C.
Tensile testing was performed at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 1000°C.
Creep testing was performed at temperatures ranging from 760°C to 1000°C.
At 760°C, the tensile yield strength and creep strength of Alloy 454 were equal to or greater than that of Mar-M 247.
The creep rupture strength of Alloy 454 showed greater strength than the reference alloys at high temperatures.
At 760°C, the tensile yield strength near the -111 to 011 axis boundary was low, about 3/4 of the strength near the 001 axis.
At 982°C, the anisotropy in creep strength was low for Alloy 454.
The Schmid factor contours for the most highly stressed slip systems were analyzed to explain the anisotropic behavior.
The high tantalum content of Alloy 454 contributed to the precipitation hardening of the gamma' phase, improving high temperature strength.
The narrow spacing between gamma' phases in Alloy 454 helped maintain the geometric arrangement even after fracture or rupture.
Intense activity of the {100}<110> slip system was observed in Alloy 454 near the -111 axis orientation.
The low creep strength near the -111 axis in Alloy 454 was attributed to the development of {100} slip between the gamma' phases.
Alloy 454 showed a schematic stereographic triangle presentation of creep strength, with the -111 and 011 axes being low strength orientations.
